I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
Come explore with me
I have a whole beautiful city to show you.
CITY OF TOMO
06

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
01
The morning had room
My name is Zeya, and I know a secret about our city: the best way to meet it
is before breakfast. That is when the river catches the peach-colored sky and
the tomato leaves wear tiny glass beads of dew.
I was already outside when Elyra opened her window. She had arrived the
evening before, and I had promised to show her my favorite places. Solara
waved from her balcony with a cup of tea. She helped build our first
gardens, so she knows stories even the oldest trees might enjoy.
At the gate, TOMO was waiting for a snail to cross the path. Its two amber
eyes shone above its sturdy wheels. One little arm held a watering nozzle
very still.
“Does it always wait?” Elyra asked.
“Whenever it needs to,” I said. “The snail lives here too.”
Behind us, flowers climbed the houses. Ahead, the river curled around an
orchard, and breakfast smelled like warm bread. I opened my notebook to a
fresh page. There was so much I wanted to show Elyra that I drew a sun with
extra-long rays.
“Come on,” I told her. “We have a whole beautiful day.”
I like a morning with room for everyone.
CITY OF TOMO
07

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
02
Breakfast belonged to the day
Our breakfast tables sit beneath the grape arbor. A humanoid carries warm
idlis from the kitchen, a small delivery robot brings strawberries, and
someone is always passing the bread before you finish asking.
Elyra wondered how we paid. Solara told us the story of a city imagined as a
cruise ship: people had already helped provide its services through taxes, so
they could arrive at a table and simply eat. Shared kitchens grew from that
beginning.
“And now?” I asked, although I knew this part and loved hearing it.
“Now we care for the things that care for all of us,” Solara said.
In our city, nobody carries money. We share the gardens, homes, kitchens,
energy, and machines. The robots grow, harvest, cook, and deliver. Our local
nodes help time it all, from ripe fruit to a warm meal. We count supplies
carefully so there is enough to share.
I gave Elyra the larger half of my peach. Later there would be lunch, and
later still, soup by the pond. Breakfast belonged to the day, just as sunshine
belonged on the table.
In my notebook I drew a bowl with enough room for one more strawberry.
The loveliest thing to pass across a table is welcome.
CITY OF TOMO
08

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
03
Where the streets went
I took Elyra to the orchard overlook, where you can see two cities at once.
Through the glass below, electric vehicles travel in underground tunnels.
Freight has its own routes, and robots inspect the lights, drainage, and
walls. There are accessible entrances and clear routes for emergencies.
Above us, the old streets have become gardens and a turquoise lazy river.
You can float along the gentle current, walk beside it, or take a dry pod and
read. The paths have room for feet and wheels, and the bridges have places
to pause.
I chose a pod with a curved, clear roof. Elyra brought a book. I brought three
questions and a pear, which is almost the same amount of luggage.
A river guardian checked the water near the landing. Its node watched the
level and flow, helping keep our beautiful route ready for everyone. We
waved to a family crossing the bridge, and the pod slowed patiently.
“What is your favorite way to travel?” Elyra asked.
I considered floating, reading, and pear-eating. “Whichever one lets me see
something new.”
Just then a dragonfly landed on the canopy, and our journey gained another
passenger.
Up here, the city makes room for living.
CITY OF TOMO
09

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
The smallest beginning
I found a very big idea in one little garden.
CITY OF TOMO
10

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
04
A small robot, a particular plant
My favorite tomato plant leans toward the morning sun. I recognize its
crooked bamboo stake. TOMO recognizes much more: its place in the bed,
its identity, and the visits that belong to its story.
We watched TOMO approach the root zone and lower a probe. Its arms can
extend and fold among the stems. Beside the rosemary stood our garden
node, a little weatherproof box holding the garden's memory.
“The node remembers yesterday,” I told Elyra. “TOMO brings it today.”
The node knew about the last watering, recent rain, and a reading that
needed checking. This morning's task allowed a fresh measurement before
any water was given. TOMO measured again, then delivered a small,
recorded amount.
I drew a circle around the plant in my notebook. Later TOMO would return
to check the result. That is one of my favorite parts: care comes back to see
how things are growing.
Solara says a whole idea can begin in a very small place. Here was ours: one
remembered garden, a robot able to act, and a gentle loop of observing,
deciding, helping, and learning.
I added a red tomato to my drawing. It was still green on the plant, but I had
room for tomorrow.
A little garden can hold a very big beginning.
CITY OF TOMO
11

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
05
Many shapes of kindness
There are many robots like TOMO in our city, and I enjoy guessing what
each body is good at. A broad, low robot carries mulch over soft ground. An
orchard robot reaches fruit high above my head. Little floating robots move
among the reeds, while a crawler checks the pipes below our feet.
Humanoids use familiar tools, climb stairs, knead dough, and repair
windows. They do the heavy, repetitive, and dangerous work that keeps our
city comfortable. TOMO's wheels and delicate arms are just right for its own
corner of the world.
People make things too. Elyra tried shaping a clay bowl while I painted a
small wooden planet. We could take our time. Nobody needed to make a
living from the bowl or prove that a painted planet was useful.
At the workshop, Solara showed us spare joints and labeled parts. Robots
need care as well. Their bodies are designed to be opened, understood, and
repaired.
I drew an orchard robot beside a pond robot, then squeezed TOMO between
them. Each was a different shape, but all were helping a place flourish.
“A whole family of possibilities,” Elyra said. I liked that so much I wrote it
down.
There are so many shapes a helpful idea can take.
CITY OF TOMO

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
A question in the field
My next question might take us all the way to space.
CITY OF TOMO
13

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
06
The classroom without a bell
Our morning lesson began in the bean field. We were measuring shade when
I found a beetle beneath a leaf and asked where it slept. Soon we were
sketching tiny shelters and wondering how the afternoon light would change
them.
My companion robot held a magnifying lens steady. It could fetch
yesterday's observations and help me compare measurements. I supplied the
questions, including the ones that wandered a long way from the beans.
Under the pavilion were books, tactile models, worktables, and quiet rooms.
Some of my friends liked a clear lesson plan; some learned best while
moving. We could study mathematics through a bridge, reading through a
field journal, and history through the story of the river.
Elyra asked what I wanted to learn next. I looked at the tomato bed and then
at the pale daytime Moon.
“What would a tomato need to grow up there?”
Our teacher handed me a fresh sheet. Water, light, air, warmth, nutrients:
the list soon filled with arrows. TOMO waited beside us as though a trip to
the Moon might be its next appointment.
By lunch, the bean field had become the beginning of a space greenhouse.
One good question can open a window all the way to space.
CITY OF TOMO
14

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
07
The garden listened
I chose the garden's morning melody. It had soft, bright notes that seemed
to hop between the leaves. Elyra sat beside me while I wrote down the time,
the weather, and which experimental bed was listening.
We were studying whether particular sound treatments changed how
particular plants responded. A nearby comparison bed had similar conditions
and no added music. I loved choosing the sounds, and I loved finding out
what actually happened.
In a separate enclosure, researchers were trying targeted acoustic signals to
discourage a specific pest. They checked the effects on other creatures too.
A treatment stayed only if the evidence supported it. Flowers, protective
screens, beneficial insects, and careful gardening all had their own parts to
play.
“So your notebook gets a vote?” Elyra asked.
“The plants get the vote,” I said. “My notebook helps us listen.”
Solara smiled and checked the comparison bed. We were exploring a
possibility, one patient observation at a time.
Beyond the trial, birds were arranging a concert of their own. I left a little
space between our notes and theirs. Even a musical garden needs quiet
places, and I wanted to hear everything it had to tell us.
I can love a possibility and still be delighted to discover.
CITY OF TOMO

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
An evening beside the water
I saved a place for you beside the lanterns.
CITY OF TOMO

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
08
A table at the water
Solara reserved our evening table beneath the pink lanterns. The reservation
saved our places and helped the kitchen prepare the right amount of food.
There would be no bill after dinner.
Popular tables were shared by taking turns. If someone changed plans,
another family could enjoy the place. I liked knowing the pond would have
its lovely view tomorrow too.
A floating guardian moved across the water, gathering oxygen and
temperature readings for the pond node. Silver fish slipped beneath the
lilies. A humanoid brought tomato soup, and I wondered whether one of our
morning tomatoes had joined it.
“That is a very good journey for a tomato,” Elyra said.
At the far end of the terrace, musicians began to play. People arrived with
shawls, wheelchairs, children, and friends. Music was free at the point of
showing up, which meant the important preparation was finding a
comfortable place to listen.
I leaned my notebook against a lantern and tried drawing the sound as
colored ribbons. Solara passed the bread. Elyra stayed for another song.
The table was ours for conversation as well as dinner, and the evening still
had plenty of stars to unfold.
Some evenings are made of soup, songs, and one more story.
CITY OF TOMO
17

I · COME EXPLORE WITH ME
09
The rain joined our afternoon
The rain arrived earlier than expected, adding tiny drumbeats to the
tablecloth. I held out my hand. Upstream, a node had already noticed rising
water and sent a fresh observation toward the river district.
Our pods took another route while the lowest landing closed. A humanoid
helped carry cushions under the pavilion, and the musicians moved their
instruments where everyone could stay dry. Underground, maintenance
robots checked the drainage.
I watched the city change its plan together. Messages carried their time,
place, and uncertainty. Each guardian attended to its own patch and shared
what neighboring places needed to know.
TOMO paused the watering. Rain at our table did not tell the garden node
exactly how much had reached each root zone; fresh local readings would
help it decide.
Elyra and I stood under the roof, counting circles in the pond. Solara
brought warm tea. Soon the concert began again, with the rain adding a
wonderful soft percussion.
I opened my notebook to write that an afternoon could become more
beautiful by changing shape. Beside the words I drew a rain garden filling
gently, taking care of the water that had come to visit.
A fresh observation can lead to a lovely new plan.
CITY OF TOMO
18

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
The intelligence of care
Come see how our city remembers its places.
CITY OF TOMO
19

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
10
The box beside the rosemary
The next morning, Solara opened the garden node's cabinet for us. I peered
inside at the computer, memory, and tidy connections. It looked wonderfully
ordinary for something that knew so much about tomatoes.
Some nodes used a GPU for heavier image processing and inference. Other
gardens needed smaller computers. The size followed the job.
Our weatherproof cabinet sat on a raised pad beside the path. Nobody had
dug a data trench across the garden. Local wireless carried everyday
messages; the dock offered a physical connection as well.
Solara showed us the power supply, cooling, seals, and space for
maintenance. The box still needed reliable energy and protection from heat
and rain. Its pad kept it clear of ordinary puddles, and its placement
considered higher water too.
“A little house for remembering,” I said.
“With good ventilation,” Elyra added.
I drew tiny windows on my notebook version, although the real cabinet had
exactly the openings its design required. TOMO arrived with new
observations, and the node added them to the garden's story.
I liked that a useful beginning could be placed beside a rosemary bush. We
could build, test, and learn right here on the ground.
An ordinary box can help a whole garden flourish.
CITY OF TOMO
20

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
11
What, when, and how
I invented a little rhyme for our garden: the node remembers what and
when; TOMO works out how, and then reports again. Solara said it was a
useful beginning, so I wrote it in green.
The node held plant history, estimated conditions, and scheduled attention.
Today's goals included inspecting the shaded bed and revisiting a probe.
TOMO chose a workable approach, steered around a hose, positioned its
arm, and took measurements within the task's limits.
“Does the node tell every wheel where to turn?” Elyra asked.
I pointed to the path. “TOMO has to notice me right now if I step in front of
it.”
Immediate movement, obstacle handling, and safe stopping belonged
onboard. Motor and pump controls had their own watchdogs. Tasks also
carried permissions and expiry times, so the robot knew the boundaries of
its helpfulness.
At the pond, I found the same idea in a floating body: the node watched the
water's longer story, while the robot navigated around reeds.
That was distributed intelligence I could point to. Places kept their
memories. Robots brought capable movement. Together they could do a
thoughtful job without sending every little motion far away.
Our garden shares the thinking, and keeps the care close.
CITY OF TOMO
21

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
12
The map beneath the leaves
Solara let me open the garden map. There were paths, slopes, bed edges,
turning spaces, and the dock. Beside it, the world graph showed things and
their relationships: this tomato in that bed, this sensor near those roots, this
watering linked to yesterday's task.
The map helped TOMO move. The graph helped it connect what happened to
the right living place. They shared a coordinate frame, which meant their
different views could agree about where we were.
I drew TOMO beside a plant, leaving room for its arm. Visiting a tomato
means stopping where you can reach it gently. That small gap belongs in the
plan.
As leaves grew and chairs moved, TOMO updated what had changed. It
combined its sensors with movement estimates and checked for wheel slip or
uncertain location. A familiar garden could still bring a fresh surprise.
Elyra asked me to explain spatial intelligence. I held my hands apart to show
the space between a wheel and a stem.
“Knowing where things are, how they fit, and how to move among them,” I
said. Then I added a bridge to my drawing, because reaching someone kindly
seemed a fine use for knowing where.
Spatial intelligence helps a helpful robot arrive gently.
CITY OF TOMO
22

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
13
A seed receives an address
I held a tomato seed on my fingertip while a sowing robot prepared the soil.
Such a tiny thing could become a whole summer of leaves and fruit. I wanted
its story to begin before the first green shoot.
The node created a planting-site record: location, variety, date, and care
instructions. Later, observations of emergence would join that same record.
The plant could change its shape while its identity stayed connected to its
beginning.
TOMO's observations had identities too. Readings included units, source,
quality, and the time they were taken. The node also recorded when it
received them. Yesterday's measurement arriving today could enrich the
history while staying clearly yesterday's measurement.
Solara showed me how raw readings stayed distinct from estimates. Even an
uncertain clock had a place in the record. The garden could remember
exactly what it knew and what needed checking.
Elyra sketched the seed while I wrote its planting site beside it. Neither
drawing nor record could tell the whole future. Together they gave us a
lovely way to return and notice.
I pressed the seed gently into its new address and imagined visiting its first
leaf.
A seed begins a story we can keep coming back to.
CITY OF TOMO
23

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
14
The joy of another question
One tomato's leaves drooped after the rain, although the probe suggested
wet soil. I brought Elyra over to see. TOMO gathered a closer look, and the
node kept both observations together.
“What could we learn next?” Solara asked.
I suggested checking the sensor. Elyra wondered whether water drained
differently across the bed. We planned another measurement at a checked
depth and an inspection of the probe. A good question could help us choose
the most useful visit.
The node used a simple water-balance model: water delivered, rain reaching
the roots, estimated losses, and drainage. It compared the prediction with
fresh readings. Differences showed us where more attention might help.
Similar past cases could be found through vector retrieval. The world graph
linked them to their plants, conditions, and outcomes. A resemblance offered
evidence to consider; the watering decision still needed the right local
context.
I liked that intelligence could include being curious. We were learning the
garden's habits without asking every leaf to tell its whole story at once.
In my notebook I drew a question mark shaped like a growing vine. At its tip
I added a little leaf.
Every useful question gives tomorrow somewhere to grow.
CITY OF TOMO
24

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
15
TOMO knew the way home
During a planned test, Solara switched off the wireless link. I watched TOMO
continue an approved inspection, carrying its current tasks and
completed-action records in durable onboard memory.
A watering step needed fresh authorization, so TOMO saved that part for later.
It watched its energy reserve and followed its own map toward the shed. When
a branch crossed the path, it paused and chose a safe way forward.
“It brought the useful thinking along,” I told Elyra.
At the dock, a local reference helped TOMO line up. Contact confirmed arrival.
The connector supplied power and a physical data path, letting the robot and
node share the records the radio had not carried.
Each task had an identity. The node and robot checked what had actually been
done before deciding what came next. A watering amount that remained
uncertain would be assessed before another delivery.
Solara cleaned the connector and checked the return-path notes. Good
fallbacks needed practice and maintenance, just like good journeys needed a
way home.
I drew TOMO entering its little shed with a satchel of observations. My
drawing added the satchel, of course. The real robot carried its stories in
memory.
A remembered route and a ready dock make a welcome home.
CITY OF TOMO
25

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
16
Guardians of their patches
I collected guardians in my notebook the way some people collect shells. The
pond guardian knew water levels, oxygen, and temperature. The orchard node
remembered branches and fruit. A roadside node watched the conditions
around its own bend.
Each had a patch to understand. Tiny sensors contributed observations. More
capable boxes kept local models and coordinated tasks. A neighborhood
computer could help with heavier work when needed. A node might be small
as a sensor or large as a data center; its size followed its purpose.
I drew them in a circle instead of a staircase.
Nearby nodes could relay useful updates. Groups might choose a leader for a
shared task, then organize differently for the next one. The whole planet did
not need a single master watching every leaf.
The river warning could travel to a bridge. Private household information
could stay at home. Permissions, freshness, and relevance helped decide what
to share.
Elyra watched a pond robot turn beside a lily. “So each place gets attention
close by.”
I nodded and added one more lily to my page. The guardians helped our places
flourish while we enjoyed the wonderful business of living among them.
Every patch can have its own thoughtful kind of attention.
CITY OF TOMO
26

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
17
A planetary nervous system
I covered the workshop wall with a drawing of our city as a constellation.
Garden, pond, bridge, kitchen, orchard: each place had a bright circle, and
every useful connection became a line.
Solara called the bigger idea a planetary nervous system. Local intelligence
stayed grounded in its own place while sharing observations that could help
another. A weather change traveled toward the gardens it might affect,
carrying its source, time, and uncertainty.
The world graph made relationships explicit. Vector retrieval found similar
experiences. Spatial maps helped bodies move. Models predicted change, and
observations afterward helped us learn how well those predictions worked.
I used different colors for those different jobs. Soon my constellation looked
like a festival.
Two gardens could report different rain and both be right about their own
ground. Old messages needed checking. Private nodes could share an
important warning while keeping other information local.
Elyra helped me extend the drawing beyond the paper, imagining a
neighboring district and another green circle farther away.
However large the network became, every circle meant a place worth
understanding. I put a tiny tomato at the center of mine. Great journeys can
begin with something small enough to hold.
I imagine a connected planet, bright with local understanding.
CITY OF TOMO
27

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
18
The city kept enough memory
My notebook had become very full, so I asked Solara how the garden kept all
its memories. She showed me how ordinary repeated observations could
become useful summaries, while important changes and action records
stayed available for careful study.
Models had versions and a record of their evidence. A small database could
hold readings, relationships, tasks, and history at the beginning. More
elaborate services arrived when measurements showed a reason for them.
Optional cloud archives helped with longer-term study, while daily care
stayed close to the roots. TOMO carried the computing needed for
navigation and immediate safety. The node held the longer story and
planning that several robots could share.
We checked storage, power, and temperature as carefully as water. A GPU
belonged where its work justified its energy and cooling. The builders
measured the complete arrangement before deciding how much it saved.
Elyra helped me make a summary of our own discoveries. I kept the
drawings that taught me something new and placed the others in a folder.
Enough memory could be rich, clear, and thoughtfully arranged. I left a fresh
page for tomorrow. TOMO was already bringing back something worth
remembering.
A well-kept memory leaves room for the next discovery.
CITY OF TOMO
28

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
19
How the beautiful stayed
possible
The resource room was one of my favorite surprises for Elyra. Its display
showed water reserves, stored food, energy, spare parts, and the condition of
shared machines. There were no prices beside them.
Our robots tended fields, harvested fruit, cooked meals, and delivered what
people needed. Local nodes helped time the work. Reservations guided kitchen
batches, with room for visitors who arrived without a plan. Extra fruit became
preserves for another season.
Electricity came from maintained local generation, storage, and connected
supplies. Water moved through treatment and reuse systems suited to its next
purpose. Even the river's beauty had practical companions: clean flow, flood
protection, accessible landings, and energy for its equipment.
“So someone counts all the things that help us share?” Elyra asked.
“Yes,” I said. “We can take care of enough together.”
When harvests changed, menus changed. Popular experiences used fair turns.
Food and a home remained shared foundations for everyone.
At the kitchen, a robot stirred a soup made from what had ripened that
morning. Solara let me taste it. I added a little herb and wrote the recipe in my
notebook, because stewardship could be delicious too.
Our beautiful days grow from things we tend together.
CITY OF TOMO
29

II · THE CITY SHARES ITS SECRETS
20
The first garden was smaller
In the old workshop, I found a photograph of the first trial bed. A few tomato
plants, a marked path, a node, a dock, and one robot filled the frame. Someone
stood nearby holding a notebook. I felt an immediate friendship with that
notebook.
Solara told us how the first complete loop began: find the same plant, gather a
trustworthy observation, deliver a controlled amount of water, record the
result, and return. Skilled sowing and harvesting would follow reliable
movement and watering.
The builders measured sensors and water delivery at the bench. They checked
navigation, docking, and contacts. Proposed care decisions ran in shadow mode
before they controlled the pump. Planned radio outages tested local operation,
return navigation, physical synchronization, and careful handling of uncertain
actions.
Two nodes shared one useful update before the network grew. Each trial had
criteria agreed beforehand and a record of conditions, results, and human help.
“A whole city started here?” Elyra asked.
“A whole direction,” Solara said.
TOMO was the smallest complete instance of the idea. I drew the photograph's
little garden at the bottom of my city map and gave it the brightest green I
owned.
A small, honest beginning gives a beautiful future somewhere to start.
CITY OF TOMO
30

III · MY NOTEBOOK REACHES THE STARS
Toward the stars
We are planting knowledge for a spacefaring generation.
CITY OF TOMO
31

III · MY NOTEBOOK REACHES THE STARS
21
The generation that planted
departure
Our observatory stands above a greenhouse. To reach the telescope, I walk
past warm tomato vines, which seems exactly the right route to the stars.
For our space-habitat project, Elyra helped me list questions. Where would the
water return? How would a robot find its dock through a communication
interruption? Which parts could the travelers repair? What would their
greenhouse remember?
Solara says ours is a generation building for a spacefaring generation. Some of
us may travel; some may plant the knowledge that carries others. Reliable
care, local intelligence, shared memory, and repairable machines all belong in
that inheritance.
I made a model with an orbital node remembering the greenhouse and a little
TOMO tending its plants. Other nodes marked stations and service points. A
traveling craft carried its own world model and exchanged useful information
when it reached another place.
I looked from the model to the real leaves below us. A reservoir, a valve, a
root, a lamp: the questions of a faraway home could begin here.
When my turn came at the telescope, I imagined someone tasting a tomato
under another sky. I hoped our careful garden notes would help it be delicious.
I am growing a little knowledge for someone’s great journey.
CITY OF TOMO
32

III · MY NOTEBOOK REACHES THE STARS
22
Stations among the stars
That night I dreamed I was aboard a spacecraft approaching a service
station. TOMO was with me, looking entirely at home beside a small
greenhouse full of tomato vines.
The craft had watched its reserves and kept a record of our journey. A
satellite node shared local traffic, docking references, and equipment
conditions. We checked the source and age of each message before using it.
I pictured a chain of places, each holding its own local knowledge. At a
compatible dock, a station's real power system could replenish stored
energy. Other journeys needed propellant or supplies, provided by the right
hardware and resources. The nodes helped coordinate what was actually
there.
Elyra floated to the window in my dream, and Solara handed me a ripe
tomato. Earth curved blue and bright beyond the glass.
The station's records included repairs and useful lessons from earlier
visitors. Someone had prepared this welcome before we arrived. Perhaps we
would improve it for the next craft.
In the morning I drew a little light beside every station on my map. I knew
the journey would need careful engineering. I also knew what I wanted those
lights to mean: a good place to arrive.
Somewhere ahead, another little light can be waiting.
CITY OF TOMO
33

III · MY NOTEBOOK REACHES THE STARS
23
The things I want to carry
For the departure exhibition, we each chose what a future city should send
into space. I began with seeds, water systems, tools, spare parts, medicine,
power, and maps. Then I added a library and music.
Elyra suggested a long table. Solara added an empty chair for the
unexpected guest. I drew a window with a soft seat, where someone could
simply watch the stars.
Our robots could perform the necessary labor of a habitat. People would
have time to discover, invent, play, make art, care for one another, and
wonder. I wanted us to carry those possibilities as thoughtfully as we packed
our equipment.
The generation building the journey might leave tested joints, diagrams,
repaired ideas, and lessons about sharing a small world. We could pass on
ways of living as well as ways of traveling.
Under the greenhouse glass, our teacher helped a younger child tie a shoe
while a companion robot held the drawings safe. I added that moment to my
page.
It was a small thing to pack, but I thought it belonged near the top of the list.
Wherever we went, I wanted us to know how to help someone get ready for
their next step.
I want kindness to travel with us.

IV · THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS WE SHARE
24
A celebration with room for
everyone
After the river-restoration celebration, I asked Solara who had made the
biggest difference. She invited me to walk along the bank and find all the
kinds of help that had met there.
We saw plants holding the soil, sensors reading the water, and a path wide
enough for everyone. Robots had carried stone and cleared debris. People
had shared ideas, checked drawings, welcomed neighbors, and listened to
what the place needed.
Elyra pointed to a shaded seat someone had suggested for tired walkers. I
had passed it a hundred times without knowing whose idea it was. I sat down
and appreciated it very much.
We thanked people for particular gifts. We told stories about what had
helped, and kept notes for the next project. There was so much to notice that
a single ranking would have left most of the beauty out.
I drew the river as a ribbon woven from many colors. Some threads were
easy to see; others held the edges together quietly.
That evening I decided my next question would be: what can I add to this
lovely place? I already had an idea involving flowers beside the new seat.
A shared achievement can hold a whole constellation of gifts.

The joy of being appreciated
Everyone knew Solara's stories about the earliest kitchens. People loved
hearing how a shared meal had grown into a way of caring for a city. I liked
seeing her smile when someone thanked her.
“Does being well known give you the first table?” I asked.
Solara laughed. “It gives me people to wave to while I wait my turn.”
The people who helped plan meals had a clear responsibility, shared records,
and ways for others to ask questions. They could pass that responsibility on.
Appreciation stayed a gift between people, while dinner belonged to
everyone.
Our city kept useful measures of water, energy, and machine reliability. It
did not give each person a contribution score. A kind act could be enjoyed
without becoming a number to wear.
Elyra and I helped arrange flowers for the evening. I chose the bright orange
ones; she found a blue vase. Solara washed a bowl beside a humanoid
stacking clean plates.
I thought how pleasant it was to admire someone and still stand beside her
as an equal at the sink. We could celebrate a wonderful contribution while
keeping every person welcome at the table.
Gratitude can shine without becoming a ladder.

The bench beneath the fig tree
There is a bench beneath the fig tree with a view of the river. Some days I
read there. Some days I watch the shadows move over the water and let my
notebook stay closed.
One afternoon Elyra joined me with two glasses of lemonade. We talked
about clouds shaped like spacecraft, then grew quiet enough to hear the
leaves. A man at the other end of the bench smiled as a little pond robot
passed.
Nobody needed an invitation to the shade. Dinner would be ready later. A
home, care, and time to rest belonged to our lives in every season: when we
were inventing something exciting, learning slowly, healing, or simply
enjoying an afternoon.
I liked knowing that our city had room for all those ways of being. We could
offer help with open hands because belonging was already there beneath us.
Before we left, I put a fallen fig leaf between two notebook pages. It made a
perfect heart if you looked at it sideways.
Elyra said I could make a whole book from things I noticed on that bench. I
told her I might begin tomorrow. Today I was enjoying the view.
Even a quiet afternoon belongs in a beautiful life.

What we can make possible
My model bridge looked lovely, but its middle dipped when a delivery robot
tried to cross. Elyra had made a stronger joint in hers. I carried my bridge
over and asked how she had done it.
We measured the robot's wheels together. I showed her how my painted
sides could fold outward. Soon we were building one bridge from both ideas,
broad enough for the robot and bright with my improbable flowers.
Solara brought a basket of tomatoes for the first crossing. TOMO
approached slowly, rolled over the span, and arrived beside us with its red
cargo perfectly settled.
I clapped so hard I almost dropped my notebook.
There was no prize waiting at the far end. We shared the tomatoes, admired
the bridge, and wrote down what had worked. Elyra's strong joint had
helped my flowers reach the other bank. My folding sides had made room for
a wider load.
I could still enjoy improving my own ideas. I also loved the new question our
afternoon had given me: what could we make possible together?
I drew both our hands beside the bridge, then added TOMO's little arm
holding a tomato. The drawing looked exactly as cheerful as I felt.
Together, our ideas can carry something wonderful.

IV · THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS WE SHARE
28
The freedom to give kindly
Elyra told me she wanted to stay in our city. She liked the gardens and river,
of course, but she also liked how freely people could choose their days.
Our shared food, homes, essential energy, care, and learning made a steady
beginning for every life. A person could rest, explore an idea, change
direction, or say no to an invitation, and still belong at breakfast tomorrow.
Solara said that was why the machines mattered. Their labor helped provide
the things people needed, loosening the dependencies that had once given
some people power over others' everyday lives. Common foundations left
more room for honest choices and generous relationships.
I thought of offering half my peach because I wanted to share it. I liked a
kindness that could stand on its own little feet.
“What will you do first?” I asked Elyra.
“Plant something on my windowsill.”
We visited the greenhouse to choose a seedling. TOMO waited at the gate
for a snail, and I waited beside it. The afternoon held plenty of time for
planting.
When the path was clear, I carried the seedling toward Elyra's new home,
imagining the first leaf turning to her window.
A secure beginning leaves so much room for a generous day.

IV · THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS WE SHARE
29
Make life beautiful
Tonight I am writing beside my window. Elyra's little plant is on the sill next
door. Below us, lantern light travels along the river, and the gardens smell of
jasmine and warm earth.
A kitchen humanoid puts away the last bowls. An orchard robot returns with
empty baskets. The pond guardian records a quiet reading. In a box beside
the rosemary, the node adds today's observations to the garden's memory.
TOMO comes home from the tomato bed. Tomorrow it will find a new leaf,
another measurement, another chance to help. There are many robots like
TOMO across our city, with different bodies and a shared place in the care
that makes our days possible.
Solara is at the observatory, where our space-habitat drawings are ready for
morning. I imagine the generation that will travel outward, carrying the
careful beginnings we are planting here.
On my last notebook page, I draw a garden, a star, and a long table. Then I
leave space for whatever I discover next.
The workshop door has four words painted beneath its climbing rose. They
are my favorite words to carry into tomorrow.
Make life beautiful.
Tomorrow, I will find another beautiful place to begin.

About this imagined city
City of Tomo imagines a future through the eyes of Zeya, a curious child exploring gardens,
intelligent places, friendship, and space. Elyra is her new friend and fellow explorer; Solara is
a guide and an early city builder. Their story brings Ilakkuvaselvi Manoharan's TOMO
concepts into a fictional city of shared provision and possibility.
The engineering passages adapt TOMO: The Planetary Nervous System, its talking points
and narrated-presentation script, and TOMO: Technical Architecture with its technical
talking points. These describe proposed architecture and validation work. Today's starting
point is supervised mapping, inspection, and controlled watering. The book imagines later
skilled manipulation, city-scale systems, and space habitats.
The sound garden explores experimental possibilities rather than established crop or
pest-control performance. Its comparison beds and bounded trials reflect the need to test
specific effects. Ground-level nodes require suitable power, cooling, weather protection,
communications, and maintenance. Orbital servicing requires compatible hardware, energy,
and supplies.
The narrative also develops the ideas supplied for this book about shared abundance,
contribution, distributed intelligence, and a spacefaring generation. Original X posts were
not independently retrieved; the story includes no invented post quotations. Characters and
scenes are fictional. The illustrations are AI-assisted concept art, rather than engineering
drawings or prototype photographs.
